# **Can crypto re-democratize investing?**

The greatest stock market investment of all time got off to a slow start.

Home Depot had hoped to open four stores in its first year of operation, 1979, but raised enough seed money to open only two. 

Even then, they didn’t have nearly enough cash left to stock the shelves. 

To keep the store from looking entirely barren, co-founder Pat Farrah asked suppliers to send them empty boxes. With their labels facing outward, the boxes gave customers the mistaken impression there was plenty of everything on offer.

Not that there were many customers to impress. Another co-founder, Bernie Marcus, spent the first few days after opening in the mall parking lot offering passersby $1 bills just to go in and have a look around.

Two years later, Home Depot listed on Nasdaq.

It typically takes a lot longer these days. SpaceX, for example, remained private for 24 years before offering shares to the public. 

In the June IPO, public investors bought into a company that’s launched 114 rockets so far this year, operates over 11,000 orbiting satellites, has 12 million Starlink subscribers, runs 1.4 gigawatts of data center capacity, and expects to hit $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year.

Investors in the Home Depot IPO bought into a chain of four hardware stores.

It was not an easy sell.

81172.subject: Stablecoin Blacklists Recovered Nothing in 60 Exploits
81172.body:
**gm, Defiers!**

These are the biggest stories in DeFi and crypto:

* **[Blockaid](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/issuer-blacklists-recovered-nothing-in-60-crypto-exploits-blockaid-finds)**[: blacklists recovered $0 in 60 exploits](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/issuer-blacklists-recovered-nothing-in-60-crypto-exploits-blockaid-finds)

* **[Ethereum](https://thedefiant.io/news/blockchains/ethereum-staking-hits-record-43-8-million-eth-bitwise-says)**[ staking hit a record 43.8M ETH](https://thedefiant.io/news/blockchains/ethereum-staking-hits-record-43-8-million-eth-bitwise-says)

* **[Extended](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/extended-plans-oct-22-settlement-move-from-starknet-to-arc)**[ moves from Starknet to Arc Oct. 22](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/extended-plans-oct-22-settlement-move-from-starknet-to-arc)

* **[Liquid](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/liquid-says-bitcoin-swaps-are-restored-while-peg-outs-stay-frozen)**[ reopened swaps; peg-outs stay frozen](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/liquid-says-bitcoin-swaps-are-restored-while-peg-outs-stay-frozen)

* **[Utah](https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/utah-sues-kalshi-and-susquehanna-firms-to-halt-alleged-illegal-betting)**[ sued Kalshi and Susquehanna](https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/utah-sues-kalshi-and-susquehanna-firms-to-halt-alleged-illegal-betting)

When crypto is stolen, the first call usually goes to a stablecoin issuer. Tether and Circle can add an address to a blacklist in one transaction, and the tokens at that address stop moving. A blacklist does not return the money; it only holds it in place. Today Blockaid, a blockchain security firm, published a count of what those freezes achieved this year. Who can actually stop stolen crypto, and does a freeze ever pay victims back?

Blockaid traced 60 exploits between Jan. 5 and Aug. 5 that took $1.18 billion. So far, [$9.8 million has been returned](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/issuer-blacklists-recovered-nothing-in-60-crypto-exploits-blockaid-finds) to victims, or 0.8%. Another $81.4 million is frozen but not returned. An issuer blacklist was available in 16 of the incidents and used in none of them. In 19 incidents, $97.2 million still sits where a named party could freeze it, and no one has. The stolen funds started moving a median of 17 minutes after each exploit.

The money that was held came from controls inside protocols and chains. They account for 99% of the $91.2 million frozen or recovered. Arbitrum's Security Council froze $71 million after the KelpDAO exploit. Syscoin burned $9 million of tokens its attacker had minted. Stellar's top validators rejected transactions from attacker accounts and held about $6.9 million.

The Drift case shows the limit of an issuer freeze. Drift lost $295.7 million in April, and much of it is now ETH, which has no issuer to call. Today a Drift-linked wallet [sent 23,000 ETH, about $54.8 million, into Tornado Cash](https://thedefiant.io/news/hacks/drift-linke

Last week we launched Gemini 4 Argon, our new frontier model, globally to developers and enterprises via the Gemini API, and to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, AI Studio, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search. Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It’s also our first frontier model since Koray Kavukcuoglu stepped into a new role as SVP of Google DeepMind, leading all Gemini model development, frontier AI research, and the Gemini app and developer teams. In this special edition of our newsletter, we sat down with Koray to learn more about Argon and what he sees for the future of AI. With early generations, models were largely information sources — you asked a question, got an answer, and the interaction ended there. With Gemini 4 Argon, you should increasingly feel the shift from querying to deep collaboration. With Argon, we built a trusted collaborator that takes action and stays with you through complex problems. Instead of just helping you write a snippet of code or summarize a document, Argon can navigate massive systems, use tools, and execute multi-step workflows over long horizons without losing the thread. Why is Argon fundamentally better at this? Because we focused heavily on software engineering and agentic reasoning as root multipliers. When a model truly understands how to act like a software engineer — how to plan, call functions, handle real-world ambiguity, and verify its own work — that intelligence generalizes and transfers across domains. That is why you see Argon excelling not only at complex codebase migrations and debugging, but also leading across finance, legal, cybersecurity, and scientific discovery, and even as a writing partner. Getting to this level of reliability required a philosophical shift in how we build: realizing that no benchmark will ever give you human trust. Benchmarks are a useful yardstick, but they only measure symptoms at a single point in time. To build Argon, we paired our largest-ever pre-training and reinforcement learning scale with continuous, real-world product feedback — starting with our own teams using it every day on their hardest problems.
